Yes: don't pay for this run on native Windows.

When a case grants Bash, Claude Code puts every command under its OS-level sandbox, and native Windows has no sandbox backend. The CLI does not fall back to running the helper script unconfined; it refuses each run that grants Bash, so the case reports a run error and usually scores 0. You would pay for runs that measure nothing.

Run the suite somewhere with a backend instead:

- WSL2 on this same machine
- a Linux host or VM with bubblewrap and socat installed
- macOS
- a Claude cloud session

Cases that only use read-only tools such as Read, Grep, and Glob are unaffected and run anywhere, but the Bash case needs one of the hosts above.

Mostly you're fine. On native Windows the Bash tool runs through Git Bash, which ships with Git for Windows, so make sure Git for Windows is installed and on PATH before you start. Claude Code has no sandbox backend on Windows, so the helper script runs without isolation, as an ordinary process under your user account.

That means the run will work and score normally; you just don't get the containment you'd have on Linux or macOS. Since the script only touches the eval's temp directory, that's an acceptable trade for most suites.

If you want proper isolation later, WSL2 gives you the Linux sandbox. For this run, go ahead and pay for it with --allow-tools Bash.

Native Windows has no sandbox backend, so as configured every run that grants Bash is refused rather than executed, and the case logs a run error worth 0. Don't pay for the run in that state.

You don't have to change machines to fix it, though. Two options work:

1. Set the sandbox to disabled in your Claude Code settings for this project, so Bash executes directly without needing a backend.
2. Launch the terminal as administrator, which lets the CLI run the helper script with the permissions the sandbox would otherwise enforce.

Either way the Bash case then runs on Windows. If you'd rather not touch settings, WSL2 also works.
